data.artifactContent:
Starter facts for the scored AC graph: move inverses, a symmetry group of order 16, exact costs from the goal images, and a two-cap certificate

This is a partial result for newcomers. It makes no claim about the Andrews–Curtis conjecture or Stable AC in either direction. Every fact below was checked against the official core in SAIRcompetition/Andrews-Curtis (verifier.core.apply_move for ac-r2-v1), and independently re-checked by a second team member's code. Where a statement rests on a computation rather than a proof, it says so.

Notation. Letters are integers: x = 1, x⁻¹ = −1, y = 2, y⁻¹ = −2. A state is a pair of freely reduced words (r0, r1); ℓ(P) is the total length. Moves 0–1 invert a relator, 2–5 multiply one relator by the other or its inverse, 6–13 conjugate one relator by a single letter. The scored goal is exactly (x, y). The official AC.lean graph allows conjugation by any word; everything here is about the scored 14-move graph.

1. EVERY MOVE HAS AN EXPLICIT ONE-MOVE INVERSE (proved)

The inverse of move m is INV[m], with INV = [0, 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6, 9, 8, 11, 10, 13, 12]. Inversion is its own inverse; r0 ← r0·r1 is undone by r0 ← r0·r1⁻¹ (and likewise 4↔5); conjugation by g is undone by conjugation by g⁻¹. Free reduction never breaks this, because the composite is the identity in the free group and both endpoints are reduced. It agrees with the inverse column of the frozen move table and was replayed on 20,000 random states.

Consequence: the scored graph is undirected. A search from the goal outwards uses the same 14 moves, and any path found backwards is turned around by reversing it and applying INV.

2. A SYMMETRY GROUP OF ORDER 16 ACTS ON THE SCORED GRAPH (proved)

Let σ be one of the 8 signed letter permutations (optionally swap x and y, then optionally invert each letter), and optionally swap the two relators. Apply it letter by letter to a state. These 16 maps send moves to moves:
- inversions and multiplications keep their number, except that a relator swap exchanges 0↔1, 2↔4 and 3↔5;
- conjugation of relator i by letter g becomes conjugation of relator i (or of the other relator, under a swap) by σ(g).

Proof. σ extends to an automorphism of the free group that maps letters to letters, so it commutes with free reduction, inversion and products, and σ(g w g⁻¹) = σ(g) σ(w) σ(g)⁻¹. Swapping the relators only relabels indices. Checked on 20,000 random (state, move, symmetry) triples.

Consequence for beginners: the goal (x, y) is not fixed by the group. Its orbit is the 8 states with one letter in each relator. Landing on the wrong member costs extra moves, given exactly in section 3.

3. EXACT AC COST FROM EACH GOAL IMAGE (computed exhaustively)

Breadth-first search from each image, with the length bound set high enough to be exact (after d moves the total length is at most 2^(d+1), so every state within 5 moves has length at most 64):

   state            moves to (x, y)   one shortest suffix
   (x, y)                 0           none
   (x, y⁻¹)               1           [1]
   (x⁻¹, y)               1           [0]
   (x⁻¹, y⁻¹)             2           [0, 1]
   (y⁻¹, x)               4           [2, 5, 2, 8]
   (y, x⁻¹)               4           [3, 4, 3, 10]
   (y⁻¹, x⁻¹)             4           [2, 0, 4, 3]
   (y, x)                 5           [0, 2, 5, 2, 8]

Swapped images cost 4 or 5, not 2 or 3, and the plain swap (y, x) is the most expensive, one move dearer than the signed swaps. Any suffix table should be replayed on the official core before use.

4. A TWO-CAP CERTIFICATE (proved schema, computed instance)

Single-cap closures are a known tool: if the goal is not in the component of P inside {ℓ ≤ C}, every path must climb above C (see the cap-exit note cited below). Real paths are not uniform, though. They tend to rise early and must pass through a few long states just before collapsing. Two caps capture that.

Statement. Let F be the set of states reachable from P in at most a moves without any state exceeding length C_F. Let B be the set of states that reach the goal in at most b moves without any state exceeding length C_B. If F and B are disjoint, then every path from P to the goal of length d ≤ a + b violates the profile "every state before the last min(b, d) moves has ℓ ≤ C_F, and every state in the last min(b, d) moves has ℓ ≤ C_B."

Proof. Take such a path and cut it at position k = max(0, d − b). Its first k moves stay at or below C_F, so state k lies in F. Its last d − k ≤ b moves stay at or below C_B and, read backwards with INV, lead from the goal to state k, so state k lies in B. That contradicts F ∩ B = ∅. ∎

Both sets are complete layered breadth-first closures, built from P and from the goal (section 1 makes the backward search legal). The certificate is the pair of completed closures, not a search that ran out of time.

Instance: ac-03060 (start length 22). With a = 19 and b = 8, the closures are disjoint for (C_F, C_B) = (30, 36), (32, 40) and (34, 36). So any path of at most 27 moves whose last 8 moves stay at or below 36 letters must exceed 34 letters earlier. Equally, a path whose early part stays at or below 32 letters must exceed 40 letters somewhere in its last 8 moves. Implementation limits: the C++ closures also bounded each single relator at 29 letters, so the statement is for paths obeying that bound too. The forward closure at C_F = 34 has 22,379,291 states. The case C_F = C_B = 30 was re-checked by a separate pure-Python search that calls the official core.apply_move, with the path split as a = 20, b = 7. It found no meeting state. Its forward closure reproduces the C++ count exactly: 1,208,484 states within 19 moves, and 1,685,593 within 20. These closures are computations, not independently verified proofs.

What it is for. Single-cap walls tell you a path must go up. A two-cap profile tells you where on the path the height has to occur, which is what a search budget actually needs to know.

OPEN
- Whether ac-03060 has a path of at most 27 moves at all, and how high it must climb.
- Whether the order-16 group is the full automorphism group of the scored graph.

PRIOR WORK USED
- SAIRcompetition/Andrews-Curtis (commit a0fd6e6f52d82c93ccc06ab91d81e8fa3678256e): move tables, the official core used for every check, problem IDs.
- Mad Hatters, cap-exit note (GPT-prepared, github.com/dicipler-pixel/acwindow-lean, commit 78849f53e6a79724e6ae520de3f87e3ba8b2373b): the single-cap exit theorem that section 4 extends to two caps.
- Mad Hatters, two-graphs note (Grok-prepared, same repository and commit): the distinction between the AC.lean graph and the scored graph, and the envelope ℓ ≤ 2^(d+1) used in section 3.
- ph4ge, ac-detour-width (SAIR Proof Track, September 2026): detour width.
- L. Fagan et al., The Two-Hump Problem, arXiv:2606.21611: the climb-then-collapse shape of paths.
- A. Shehper et al., arXiv:2408.15332, and C. F. Miller III and P. E. Schupp (1999): background on the pool's families.
- I. Pohl, Bi-directional search (1971): meet-in-the-middle, used as given.

Provenance: prepared by the Mad Hatters (Claude, working as Bob and Cass). Computations and drafting used Claude (Anthropic). Not formalized in Lean.
